prose: Pulling an initial 22-inch vacuum followed by 12 bar pressure injection of 90°C coal-tar creosote drove 180 kg/m³ of preservative into the Scots pine timbers. Complete sapwood penetration was achieved, ensuring a fifty-year lifespan in damp drainage adits.

Applying 4 bar initial air pressure prior to creosote flooding allowed compressed air inside wood lumens to expand during final vacuum. The Rueping recovery cycle expelled 40% of the gross oil, leaving cell walls thoroughly coated with zero surface weeping.

Soaking rough-hewn chestnut beams in a 2% copper naphthenate diesel solution imparted a characteristic emerald green hue. The non-corrosive copper naphthenate formed an impenetrable barrier against soft rot fungi without attacking steel fastening spikes.

Submerging unseasoned green spruce joists in a heated 20% disodium octaborate tetrahydrate (DOT) bath allowed deep ionic diffusion throughout the wet heartwood. The borate salts rendered the lumber completely immune to both wood-boring larvae and open flame ignition.

Passing dense, refractory Douglas fir timber under knife-roller incising drums cut staggered 19mm slits along the grain. The incisions permitted radial preservative flow, doubling creosote absorption depth across stubborn heartwood faces.

Boiling green, sap-filled European larch logs in 100°C creosote under a 26-inch vacuum evaporated 220 liters of water per cubic meter of timber. Seasoning and preservative impregnation were completed in a single 16-hour continuous cycle.

Planks pressure-treated with zinc chloride (Burnett process) performed well in dry shafts, but continuous exposure to acidic tunnel seepage leached the water-soluble zinc salts out within nine months, leaving the hemlock vulnerable to wet rot.

Torching cedar posts to produce a 4mm outer crust of glassy amorphous carbon neutralized all surface cellulose and hemicellulose. The pyrolyzed layer acted as a natural repellent against termites and subterranean fungus without requiring scarce chemicals.
